# Results — Study 801 (Employee Satisfaction — the "100 Best Companies" alpha)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
**Edmans (2011): a portfolio of Fortune's "100 Best Companies to Work For" earns positive
risk-adjusted alpha** (employee satisfaction is an intangible the market underprices).
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is
dropped). Fingerprint `4116fe2691f7` (monthly total returns of the 17 basket names + SPY).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily total-return (auto-adjusted) closes → **monthly** total returns, **126 months**, 2016-01-31 → 2026-06-30 |
| Basket | **17** publicly-listed **perennial** "100 Best Companies to Work For" / World's Best Workplaces members (hand-coded, cited — see [`data.py`](../employee_satisfaction/data.py) `BASKET`): MAR, AXP, AFL, GS, HLT, CPT, ACN, SBUX, CSCO, CRM, GOOGL, INTU, ADBE, NVDA, WDAY, NOW, CDNS |
| Market | SPY total return |
| Placebo pool | **34** large-cap **survivors not selected for workplace prestige** (`CONTROL`) — the survivorship yardstick |
| Statistics | market-model (CAPM) alpha `r_basket = α + β·r_mkt`, **Newey-West (3-lag)** HAC *t* on α (the decisive number) + OLS *t*; excess-over-market mean with NW *t*; Wilson interval on the monthly win-rate; a **random survivor-basket** placebo (5,000 draws); a first/second-half split |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention: set equal weights at the **month-end close**, earn next month; cost = one-way × NAV × realised turnover; **long-only, no borrow** |
| Adjustment | **total-return** (auto-adjusted closes) throughout — dividends folded in on every leg |

**Survivorship is named on the Signal axis, not buried.** This basket is *hand-picked from
today's known winners* — companies that stayed listed, stayed public, and stayed
great-to-work-for long enough to be recognisable in 2026. That is a textbook survivor
selection and it biases the raw comparison **toward** the basket. Perennial members that left
the tape are **excluded** and named in [`data.py`](../employee_satisfaction/data.py)
`DELISTED`: Whole Foods (Amazon, 2017), Ultimate Software (private, 2019), **Nordstrom (JWN,
taken private 2025 — it dropped out of our fetch mid-build, a live survivorship event)**, plus
private perennials (SAS, Wegmans, Publix, Edward Jones). We also control only for the **market**
(CAPM), not Edmans' 4-factor model, so a positive alpha here is an **upper bound** on any true
satisfaction alpha.

## The headline — equal-weight basket vs the market

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| basket annualized return | **+20.16%** (vol 19.4%) |
| market (SPY) annualized return | +15.02% (vol 15.2%) |
| CAPM **β** | **1.15** |
| CAPM **α** | +23.2 bps/mo = **+2.82%/yr** |
| α **Newey-West *t*** | **+1.10** |
| α OLS *t* | +1.06 |
| excess-over-market (basket − SPY) | +42.8 bps/mo |
| excess NW *t* / OLS *t* | **+1.90** / +1.96 |
| information ratio | 0.60 /yr |
| monthly win-rate vs market | 74/126 = **58.7%** (Wilson 95% [50.0%, 66.9%]) |

The basket **out-returns** the market by ~5pp/yr — but at β = 1.15, most of that gap is simply
**more market exposure**. The risk-adjusted alpha, +2.82%/yr, does **not** clear the desk bar:
NW *t* = +1.10 (OLS +1.06). The raw excess-over-market is stronger (NW *t* = +1.90) but still
sub-2, and the Wilson lower bound on the win-rate sits right on 50.0%. On the *risk-adjusted*
claim — the one Edmans actually made — this tape can't certify the effect.

## The survivorship placebo — does a random survivor basket earn alpha too?

Random equal-weight baskets of 17 large-cap **survivors not chosen for workplace prestige**
(5,000 draws from `CONTROL`), each run through the same CAPM-alpha detector:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| random survivor-basket α (mean) | **+0.20%/yr** (sd 1.18) |
| satisfaction basket α | +2.82%/yr |
| p (random survivor α ≥ basket α) | **0.013** |

This is the one genuinely favourable result: a *random* basket of known large-cap survivors
earns essentially **zero** alpha (+0.20%/yr), and only 1.3% of them match the satisfaction
basket. So the basket's edge is **not explained by survivorship + equal-weighting alone** — it
is not just "any basket of winners beats the cap-weight index". **But** the placebo controls
only for survivorship and equal-weighting, **not** for the basket's factor tilt (it is
tech/quality-heavy over a decade that richly rewarded exactly that), and the alpha itself is
statistically insignificant — so this narrows the *survivorship* explanation without
resurrecting a certified alpha.

## The tell — the alpha does not persist

First half vs second half of the 126 months:

| era | months | CAPM α | NW *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2016-01 → 2021-03 | 63 | **+8.12%/yr** | **+2.77** |
| 2021-04 → 2026-06 | 63 | **−2.25%/yr** | −0.59 |

The entire alpha lives in the **first half** (where it *does* clear the bar on its own, *t* =
+2.77) and **turns negative** in the second (*t* = −0.59). A signal that is significant in one
five-year stretch and gone-to-negative in the next is the signature of a lucky window (or a
published anomaly that decayed after Edmans 2011) — not a durable intangible premium. This is
the decisive reason the full-sample alpha is insignificant.

## The timer — hold the basket, rebalance monthly

Set equal weights at the month-end close, earn next month; cost = one-way × NAV × realised
turnover; long-only, no borrow. A buy-and-hold equal-weight basket barely trades:

| cost (one-way) | turnover | cost drag | gross α | net α | net α NW *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps | 2.4%/mo | 0.01%/yr | +2.82%/yr | **+2.81%/yr** | +1.10 |
| 10 bps | 2.4%/mo | 0.03%/yr | +2.82%/yr | **+2.79%/yr** | +1.09 |

Costs are **not** the binding constraint here — turnover is trivial. The binding constraint is
that there is **no certified alpha to harvest**: the ~5pp/yr of outperformance is β = 1.15 you
could replicate by levering SPY 1.15×, and the residual is *t* = 1.10 and non-persistent. What
looks like a paycheck is **beta you were always paid for**.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic monthly market + equal-weight basket of `β·mkt + idio` names with a plantable
monthly alpha; no network.

| world | CAPM α NW *t* |
|---|--:|
| null (alpha = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.07** (sd 0.96), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** (≈ the 5% a 2σ bar expects) |
| planted α = +40 bps/mo (seed 801) | recovered +3.98%/yr, **+2.99** |

The detector does not fire on the null (bar false-positive rate as expected) and cleanly
recovers a planted alpha. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of
the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The basket out-returns the market (+20.16% vs +15.02%/yr) and — the one
  favourable result — beats *random* survivor baskets (placebo *p* = 0.013), so the edge is
  not pure survivorship-plus-equal-weight. **But** the risk-adjusted claim Edmans actually made
  fails to clear the bar: CAPM α = +2.82%/yr at NW *t* = **+1.10** (β = 1.15 eats most of the
  raw gap), excess-over-market NW *t* = +1.90 (< 2), and the alpha is entirely **front-loaded**
  (+8.1%/yr / *t* = 2.77 in 2016-21, −2.3%/yr in 2021-26). With a hand-picked **survivor**
  basket and a market-only control, that is a WEAK signal — literature-supported, tape-unproven.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Costs are trivial (2.4%/mo turnover), but there is no certified
  alpha to bank: ~5pp/yr of outperformance is β = 1.15 (leverage you can buy directly), and the
  residual is *t* = 1.10 and non-persistent. It is beta wearing an intangible's clothes.
- **"Does the edge persist?" — BUSTED.** Significant in the first five years (*t* = 2.77),
  negative in the next (*t* = −0.59). One window, then gone.
